title: Instead Of Lowering GPU Prices, Former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang Reportedly Financed AI Startups To Absorb Excess Silicon, Shattering The Shortage Perception
body: To justify NVIDIA's need to financially underwrite OpenAI and smaller cloud operators to keep them purchasing its GPUs, Huang privately admitted that major cloud giants were pivoting away from NVIDIA in favor of in-house custom chips. With hyperscalers actively reducing their reliance on “off-the-shelf parts,” Huang acknowledged that the massive volume of prepaid TSMC wafers and memory NVIDIA had committed to buying was “coming at him like an avalanche.” [...] By funding datacenter expansion for AI startups, NVIDIA effectively created artificial demand to clear out its own surplus silicon instead of letting the supply flood the market and force GPU prices down. Those internal pressures align with earlier assessments from industry analyst Ed Zitron, who estimated that at least $200 billion worth of NVIDIA AI GPUs are sitting idle in warehouses after being purchased by cloud giants that lacked either the electrical grid capacity or immediate end-user [...] Knowing that the imminent avalanche would be upon NVIDIA sooner rather than later, the company reportedly contacted TSMC to wind down its upcoming chip orders. For PC builders and hardware enthusiasts who have endured years of steep GPU and RAM pricing under the impression of severe component scarcity, the disclosures shatter the shortage narrative and expose the aggressive financial maneuvering used to keep hardware prices elevated.

title: EU Ministers Push New Chips Strategy to Reduce Europe’s Dependence on Foreign Semiconductors - eutoday.net
body: # EU Ministers Push New Chips Strategy to Reduce Europe’s Dependence on Foreign Semiconductors. #### EU industry ministers are debating a second European Chips Act as Brussels seeks to reduce dependence on foreign semiconductor suppliers. European Union industry ministers are examining plans to reduce the bloc’s dependence on foreign semiconductor suppliers as the Competitiveness Council debates the proposed **European Chips Act 2.0** in Brussels on Thursday. The discussion forms part of a wider meeting at which ministers are also considering how to embed economic security more deeply into EU competitiveness policy, while the Commission is briefing governments on strategic projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act. The agenda brings semiconductors, industrial policy and access to critical materials into the same economic-security debate. The Commission’s impact assessment identifies dependence on a small number of third-country suppliers for semiconductor design and manufacturing as one of the central vulnerabilities addressed by Chips Act 2.0.

title: In the shadow of U.S. export controls, China rallies its own chip industry - WXXI News
body: # In the shadow of U.S. export controls, China rallies its own chip industry. In a speech at the expo, Wang ticked through the challenges: China can't buy the best graphics processing unit (GPU) chips for AI data centers; it's blocked from acquiring high-end chipmaking equipment; it faces cloud computing restrictions; state-of-the-art AI software is geared for foreign chips. And some have been puzzling over the Trump administration's decision this month to roll back some chip restrictions and allow California-based Nvidia to sell one of its best GPUs — the H200 — to China. Administration officials have argued that allowing China access to good — but not cutting-edge — chips from the United States would keep it hooked on U.S. technology and dampen China's drive for chip independence.

title: Commerce closes China’s backdoor to Nvidia chips after White House steps in - Politico
body: # Commerce closes China’s backdoor to Nvidia chips after White House steps in. A press release announcing the new rule said it was written at "the direction of Department of Treasury and the National Security Council.". The Commerce Department took steps Monday to prevent companies in restricted countries from renting advanced AI computing power from data centers abroad — a blow to tech giant Nvidia, whose chips fill those data centers. In an interim final rule expected for publication in the Federal Register, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security said it would require companies to apply for licenses before selling or shipping advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil — countries the rule identifies as posing a higher-than-normal risk that chips will be diverted, or rerouted, to China. The rule was written at the direction of Department of Treasury and the National Security Council, according to the press release issued by BIS.

title: Memory Chips Are in Short Supply. Why Isn't the US Ramping up Production? - IndustryWeek
body: The AI infrastructure buildout is critical to our economy, our technological leadership and our national security, and the Trump administration is right to encourage historic investments in America’s future. But as we build, Washington and industry need to address a fast-emerging constraint that could slow that progress and raise costs for American families: a shortage of memory chips. The U.S. and its closest allies, including South Korea and Japan, need to increase memory chipmaking as rapidly as possible to meet the needs of the AI data centers, consumer electronics and other industries. Until the new U.S. fabs are open and fully operational, we will not be able to have confidence in a global chip industry that can meet the ever-growing needs of the world with a significant share of output produced in the U.S. The good news is that China is a generation or two behind the U.S. in most forms of chipmaking.
